bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Duncan Grant (1885-1978) and Vanessa Bell (1879-1961) were British painters and designers associated with the Bloomsbury Group--an influential group of writers, intellectuals, philosophers and artists who lived or worked in around Bloomsbury, London in the first half of the 20th century.

Born in Aviemore, Scotland in 1885, Duncan Grant studied at the Westminster School of Art from 1902 to 1905, where he was supported in his learning by the French painter, Simon Bussy. Grant went on to develop his artistic skills in both Italy and France, spending a year studying at Jacques-Émile Blanche's Académie de La Palette school in Paris in 1906. In 1909, Grant moved to Fitzroy Square in London close to many members of what would become the Bloomsbury Group, including Virginia Woolf, then known as Virginia Stephen. The Bloomsbury Group came to have major influence on art, literature and philosophy and was at the forefront of changing ideas about sexuality, feminism and pacifism in the period. Duncan Grant was the friend, and lover, of many prominent members of the group, including Vanessa Bell, John Maynard Keynes and Lytton Strachey. In 1913, the painter and art critic Roger Fry established Omega Workshops, of which Grant and Vanessa Bell were directors. The workshops produced furniture, pottery and textiles and sought to provide an income to the young artists of the Bloomsbury Group, and others. During the First World War, Grant was a conscientious objector and he and Vanessa Bell set up a house (named Charleston) in Firle, Sussex, where they, and other conscientious objectors, lived and worked throughout and after the war. Although most of Grant's love affairs were homosexual, Grant and Bell had a daughter named Angelica in 1918, who took the name of Bell's husband, Clive Bell, with whom both Grant and Vanessa had an amicable relationship. Influenced by the Fauves and Cézanne in the first Post-Impressionist Exhibition of 1910-11, Grant spent the early part of his career working in the Post-Impressionist mold. Grant's artistic range was prodigious, with his works comprising a variety of mediums including paintings, textiles, pottery, theatre sets and costumes.

Born in London in 1879, Vanessa Bell was an artist similarly associated with the Bloomsbury Group. Although often overshadowed by her more famous sister, Virginia Woolf, Vanessa Bell was an accomplished and influential artist in her own right. Bell was educated at home, taking drawing lessons from Ebenezer Cook, before attending Sir Arthur Cope's art school in 1896. She went on to study painting at the Royal Academy in 1901. After the deaths of her parents, Bell moved to Bloomsbury where, alongside her sister and brothers, she began to socialize with members of the Bloomsbury Group. Like Grant, Bell was inspired by the Post-Impressionists, creating works with distinctive vision and bold colors and forms. Later in her career, she turned to Abstraction. From the First World War onwards, Bell lived between Charleston and London, in unconventional households which at various periods included Grant, his lovers, her husband, art critic Clive Bell, and his lover Mary Hutchison, and her two sons by Bell, Julian and Quentin, and her daughter by Grant, Angelica. Bell's children followed in their mother's creative legacy, with Julian becoming a poet, Quentin an art historian and author and Angelica an artist. Bell's creative output was extensive and eclectic, incorporating painting, photography, ceramics, fabrics, interiors, decorative screens and works on paper.

The recipients of Bell and Grant's letters, Kenneth (1903-1983) and Elizabeth "Jane" Clark (née Martin) (1902-1976), met as students at Oxford University and married in 1927. Jane was the Irish daughter of Emily Winifred Dickson, the first female Fellow of any Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland or Britain. Kenneth Clark was a prominent British art historian, aesthete, author, museum director and broadcaster. Greatly influenced by John Ruskin, Clark began his career as fine art curator at Oxford University's Ashmolean Museum, before going on to be the director of the National Gallery (at the age of 30). He remains the youngest person ever to hold the position. As Chairman of the War Artists Advisory Committee, and as an advisor to the Ministry of Information, Clark was a major influence on the exhibition and commissioning of art during the Second World War and on the production of propaganda films to support the war effort in Britain. In his post-war career, Clark expanded into broadcasting; he was one of the founders of the Independent Television Authority in 1954 and his 1969 BBC television series Civilisation is often credited with determining the scope and direction of television documentary in the latter half of the twentieth century. In the latter years of his life, he acted as a trustee of the British Museum and served as Chancellor of the University of York. One his last projects in the artistic sphere was to support a campaign to create a Turner Gallery for the Turner Bequest.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The collection comprises correspondence from the artistic partners, Duncan Grant and Vanessa Bell, to the art historian Kenneth Clark and his wife, Elizabeth "Jane" (née Martin). The correspondence was written over a course of approximately fifty years, with the earliest letter dating from circa 1920 and the latest from 1969. Seventeen letters in the collection are undated. The letters are broad in scope and give a deep insight into the artistic endeavors and personal lives of these four prominent figures of the artistic and cultural scene of twentieth century Britain.

A large portion of the collection pertain to major artistic, often collaborative, works by Duncan Grant and Vanessa Bell and reflect their eclectic creative range. Eighteen letters relate to Kenneth Clark's commission for Grant and Bell to decorate a full dinner service on the theme "Famous Women" and give an account of the discussions between the trio surrounding the commission's theme, where to have the service pieces manufactured and who the "famous women" subjects should be (see various letters from Duncan Grant and Vanessa Bell to Kenneth and Jane Clark dating from 1932 December 13 to 1933 July 26). The correspondence also gives an account of Grant and Bell's interior decoration work and details their artistic processes in designing interiors for the National Gallery Restaurant, Berwick Church, Sussex and The Devonshire Hill School, Tottenham (letters from Duncan Grant to Jane Clark, 1942 June and 1942 June 4; Vanessa Bell to Kenneth Clark 1943 March 9, and Vanessa Bell to Jane Clark 1944 March 4.) One letter references Duncan Grant's work in theater design, with Vanessa Bell informing Kenneth Clark that Grant has been kept busy working on costumes for a ballet at the Old Vic, for a run of The Enchanted Grove , opening in March 1932 (letter from Vanessa Bell to Kenneth Clark 1932 February 22). Three letters evidence the events surrounding what became known as the "Cunard Affair," an incident in which Cunard White Star Ltd. asked Duncan Grant and Vanessa Bell to submit panels to decorate their new flagship liner RMS Queen Mary. Cunard later rejected the panels, even after their completion, and denied Grant compensation claims for loss of reputation. As this correspondence demonstrates, the affair saw many prominent figures, including Kenneth Clark, vocally express their support for Grant and Bell in the national press (letters from Vanessa Bell to Kenneth Clark, 1935, 1935 April 17 and 1935 April 28). The close collaborative endeavors of both artists are reflected in their work with the Bloomsbury Group-affiliated Omega Workshops, which provided an income to a variety of artists, including Grant, Bell and Wyndham Lewis. The ethos and financial operation of the Workshops are made apparent in a letter from Vanessa Bell to Kenneth Clark where she asks Clark's advice on dealing with manufacturers and expresses her desire to support new, younger artists through the company (letter from Vanessa Bell to Kenneth Clark, 1945 March 27).

The correspondence gives details about a variety of exhibitions and artistic events taking place in and around London and Sussex (where the four were variously resident) and shows the respect Grant and Bell had for Kenneth Clark's opinion on such matters. Grant seeks Clark's advice regarding ideas Grant has had for a "modern section" of an exhibition of British artists and for a wartime exhibition of lithographs by artists including Graham Sutherland, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Eugène Delacroix, amongst others (letters from Duncan Grant to Kenneth Clark, 1937 November 17, 1945 February 23 and 1945 March 5.) Similarly, in a letter to Kenneth Clark, Vanessa Bell seeks out the "disinterested" opinion of the art historian on an exhibition of works by painter and critic Roger Fry following his death.

The high regard in which Grant and Bell held Kenneth Clark is also clear in their remarks on his criticism and ideas. Throughout their friendship, Clark sent both artists copies of his latest publications and both are enthusiastic in the feedback they give him in their letters. Two letters, sent to the Clarks on Kenneth Clark's presentation of his 1956 book The Nude: a study in ideal form to both artists, especially convey the way in which Clark influenced opinion and discussion in Grant and Bell's artistic partnership. Grant tells the Clarks that he and Bell were "delighted" by the gift, commenting that they "are all, in various degrees, interested in Sex and Art" (letter from Duncan Grant to Jane and Kenneth Clark, 1956 December 7.) In a letter to Kenneth and Jane Clark from Vanessa Bell, written the same day, Bell jovially informs Kenneth Clark that he has divided their "apparently united household" and remarks that he has "written something which is evidently going to stir us all up and make us talk and think and dispute and try to find out what we really feel about the things we care most for" (letter from Vanessa Bell to Jane and Kenneth Clark, 1956 December 7). Other letters in the collection provide an insight into Grant and Bell's responses to Clark's Looking at Pictures and Ruskin Today (letter from Duncan Grant to Kenneth Clark, 1964 December 4, and from Vanessa Bell to Kenneth Clark 1960 December 19.) However, while Bell and Grant clearly venerate Clark's ideas, the regard held by Clark for the two artists is also apparent. The influence held by their opinion on his professional decisions is perhaps discernible in a letter sent by Grant to Jane Clark in which Grant entreats her to encourage her husband to publish his studies on the work of Rembrandt. Three years later, Clark did indeed publish a book on Rembrandt, titled Rembrandt and the Italian Renaissance .

The collection provides a glimpse into the wider connections the letters' authors and recipients held in the artistic, literary and cultural world of twentieth century Britain. Throughout the correspondence, references are made to a plethora of artists, authors and other creatives who make visits to Grant and Bell, collaborate with them on projects and invite their involvement in various exhibitions and events. These acquaintances include, among others, the writer, J.R. Ackerley, critic and journalist, Desmond McCarthy and art collector, W.W. Winkworth (letter from Duncan Grant to Kenneth Clark, 1961 October 19; to Jane Clark 1949 July 28, and from Vanessa Bell to Kenneth Clark 1933 May 11). Frequently, Grant and Bell, especially, make references to "Roger," their friend and painter Roger Fry. The close relationship held between Fry, Bell, Grant and the Clarks is obvious in a letter where Bell writes to Jane Clark to say that Fry has suggested that a screen Bell is producing for Clark will not go well with the existing decoration in Clark's bedroom (letter from Vanessa Bell to Jane Clark 1933 May 24).

Broader developments and happenings in the contemporary art and manufacturing scene are discussed frequently throughout the correspondence. For instance, Grant writes to Jane Clark about her promise to finance the printing for the first prospectus for Claude Rogers and John Passmore's Euston Road School (letter from Duncan Grant to Jane Clark, 1937). References are made throughout the letters to various art dealers, galleries and institutes, including Colnaghi, Agnew's, the Lefevre Gallery and The Courtauld Institute of Art and much of Bell, Grant and the Clarks' discussion of their Famous Women Dinner Service revolves around which pottery manufacturer to use. Indeed, regarding this last topic, the letters give specific details about the operations of various prominent pottery companies including Wedgwood, Poole Pottery and The Ashtead Pottery, the last of which Bell discloses has closed "owing to hard times" (letter from Vanessa Bell to Kenneth Clark 1933 January 6). The collection items themselves are also indicative of the expansion of the mass production of art witnessed in the lead-up to the period. For instance, two of Grant's missives to Clark are written on postcard reproductions of artworks by Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot and Andrea Mantegna (postcards from Duncan Grant to Kenneth Clark, 1936 and 1942 August 8.)

Perhaps the most obvious external influence in the artistic contexts described in the correspondence is that of the Second World War and many of the letters relate to the artistic activities of the four during the conflict. Kenneth Clark was the Chairman of the War Artists' Advisory Committee, a government agency established to artistically document the war. Clark commissioned Grant to paint St Paul's Cathedral, new perspectives of which had been revealed due to bomb damage sustained during the Blitz. The new views of the city revealed by bombings are described by Grant in one letter as making London look "like Ancient Rome" (letter from Duncan Grant to Kenneth Grant, 1941). In the same year, Grant suggests to Clark that he commission Quentin Bell to create wartime agricultural works (letter from Duncan Grant to Kenneth Clark, 1941 November 29.) In addition to the production of artistic works, wartime efforts to exhibit art are evident in the correspondence. Ten letters from Duncan Grant to Kenneth Clark revolve around requests by Grant to Clark to lend pieces to Miller's, a gallery – founded by Frances Byng Stamper and Caroline Lucas – operating from 1941 to 1945 in Lewes, Sussex. The letters show that Clark was able to help the gallery exhibit works by a number of prominent artists including Constantin Brâncu?i, Henri Matisse, Pablo Picasso and Edgar Degas (letters from Duncan Grant to Kenneth Clark, 1941 November 29 and 1942 January 12.)

The collection also offers an insight into the way in which technology influenced both artistic practice and day to day life in the first half of the twentieth century. Grant's letters especially reveal how the development of photography and photographic slides changed the ways in which art was displayed, although often his writings reveal that these technologies continue to require a level of expertise. In one instance, for example, Grant writes to Kenneth Clark to change the date of a lecture he is giving in Lewes so that the chemist will be available to "manipulate the slides" (letter from Duncan Grant to Kenneth Clark, 1942 October 21). The expanding role of the telephone in facilitating everyday communication is also apparent in the letters and Vanessa Bell frequently tells the Clarks that they may "ring her up" in London if the wish to contact her and apologizes that her and Grant's Sussex home, Charleston, is not yet fitted with a telephone (letter from Vanessa Bell to Kenneth Clark, 1935 March 30, and an undated letter to Jane Clark May 29.)

The letters convey close friendships between the four and record many important and poignant moments in their personal lives. Throughout the collection, Grant and Bell send their support to the Clarks on the occasion of family illness and thank the couple for their best wishes for their own household's health, in turn. Four items stand out for the deeply emotive circumstances to which they pertain. One is a letter from Vanessa Bell to Kenneth Clark, thanking him for his sympathy note after the suicide of her sister, Virginia Woolf, in 1941. She writes that "it is a help to know that those besides those who her knew her well understand what they have lost" and encourages Clark, and the younger generation more widely, not to lose courage (letter from Vanessa Bell to Kenneth Clark 1941 April 15). Twenty years later, Grant penned similar letters to the Clarks on the death of Vanessa herself. Thanking Kenneth for his sympathy note, Grant tells his friend that letters "from people expressing their affection and admiration for Vanessa although they of course in a way add to one's sense of general loss, give one some courage to face up to one's own desolation" (letter from Duncan Grant to Kenneth Clark 1961 April 18). In a letter to Jane Clark, written the same day, Grant expresses the great pleasure that her memories of Bell have given him and notes that "several people in their letters have remembered [Bell's] sense of humour. I now realise of course that this is true but I always took it for granted" (letter from Duncan Grant to Jane Clark 1961 April 18). A letter from Grant to Jane Clark in July 1937 relays the "terrible news" of the death of the poet, and son of Vanessa and Clive Bell, Julian Bell while working with the Red Cross during the Spanish Civil War. Grant writes frankly about the effect the event has had on Vanessa Bell, who "has completely collapsed physically. She is in bed & very weak & can hardly eat anything" (letter from Duncan Grant to Jane Clark 1937 July 21). In addition to such major life events, the correspondence also provides an insight into the more quotidian subjects that the four discussed, including the country walks surrounding Charleston and recommendations for dentists (letter from Duncan Grant to Kenneth Clark 1942 October 21 and an undated letter from Vanessa Bell to Jane Clark).

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant says that two of his artist friends, Robert Lotiron and a "M. Clairin" [probably Pierre-Eugène Clairin], are looking for works to include in an exhibition of English pictures for their "Autumn Salon" [Salon d'Automne]. He says that they would like to talk to Clark about the matter and gives him their address in Queen's Gate.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell says that she and Duncan Grant would be delighted to decorate a dinner service for Clark and make him a rug. She tells him she will let him know how much she thinks it will cost and asks if Clark would like to see the design for the rug before it is made. Bell says that the kiln at Omega Workshops would be too small to make the service and that they should probably approach a large pottery firm to make it. She says it is "very enterprising" of Clark to commission the service from them and is encouraged that "in these dark times[...]anyone is bothering about such things at all."

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell informs Clark that she has finished the needlework design he has asked from her and asks him whether he would like her to trace it on to anything or send the design to him. She asks whether he would like her to pick up colored wools or silks when she returns to London. Bell says that she and Duncan Grant had hoped to be able to get Clark's commissioned decorated dinner service made by The Ashstead Pottery but that it has closed down "owing to hard times." She says they are looking into other possibilities for the pottery and suggests that they might ask Poole Pottery or Wedgwood.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell apologizes for her delay in communicating with Clark about his rug, saying that Duncan Grant has been busy designing costumes and scenery for ballet at the Old Vic [the ballet being The Enchanted Grove.] Grant has received pricing for the manufacture of Clark's rug and Bell tells Clark it will be £10, so that the whole cost of making the rug would be £15. She asks Clark to "please let [her] know if this is too much." She ends by telling Clark she hopes he has recovered from his accident. In a postscript, Bell informs Clark that she has discussed his dinner service with Roger Fry who suggests that they get the service produced by Poole Pottery or Wedgwood and Bell says that she has written to Poole about manufacturing the service.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell gives Clark more bad news about his commssion for Duncan Grant and Bell to decorate a dinner service. Poole pottery have refused to produce the set, saying it would not be worth their time to make just one. Poole recommended a "woman potter" but Bell is cautious of using this producer as she does not seem aware of the type of glaze Grant and Bell would like. Bell instead suggests they approach Wedgwood and Sons and complains that "the English manufacturers are hopeless people. They are so terribly unenterprising & have such appalling taste which they assume to be also that of the public." Bell sends Clark some wool and asks, if there is any left over, to return unused wool.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell says she "feels too ashamed" about keeping Clark waiting but tells him that his rug is now being made and that, through the intervention of W.W. Winkworth, they have got in touch with Wedgwood and Sons regarding Clark's commssion for Duncan Grant and Bell to decorate a dinner service. Wedgwoods have agreed to take part in the work and Bell and Grant are painting some specimens to see how they will work with the company's colors and glazes.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 2 sheets (3 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 25 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell informs Clark that she and Duncan Grant have visited Wedgwood's Etruria Works ceramics factory regarding Clark's commission for Duncan Grant and Bell to decorate a dinner service. They have decided on what type of plate and color they will use. Having made prototypes of some plates, they have also decided to use the underglaze on the advice of the company's art director. Bell remarks that W.W. Winkworth also accompanied them to Etruria.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 18 x 12 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell updates Clark about his commission for Duncan Grant and Bell to decorate a dinner service. Bell says that the colors on some specimen plates have come out clearly but that she and Grant don't like them very much. She asks Clark if he might be able to come and discuss "price and treatment" with her and Grant regarding the commission.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell tells Clark that Wedgwoods have not yet informed her of the price of the dinner service Clark has commissioned Duncan Grant and Bell to decorate. She asks if Clark could perhaps meet with them during the following week. Bell says it was kind of Clark to say that he liked one of her recent works at Agnew's Gallery. She says she thinks she will have to lower the prices of her works and that she and Grant would be glad if Clark owned their works. She ends by reflecting on a large picture by Grant, saying that she wishes "some public place could own it since no private houses seem big enough now."

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 2 sheets (3 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell writes to Clark to apologize for delays regarding his commission for Duncan Grant and Vanessa Bell to decorate a large dinner service. She tells him that they have sent a tea seat and some plates to be glazed and fired at Wedgwood's but that they not entirely happy with the colors and qualities of the tea set. Bell informs Clark that Wedgwood have lost the plates. Bell proposes the idea of making famous women the subjects of the work and asks if Clark likes the plan. She tells Clark that they have brought the dinner service to Charleston where they can work on it in a quiet atmosphere. Bell ends by giving Clark an account for a rug he has bought from her and Grant as follows: "1 rug 6 ft x 4 ft. £15.0.0."

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell thanks Clark for his check and letter response. She is glad he approves of the famous women theme for his dinner servive commission for Bell and Duncan Grant. Bell informs him that she and Grant has begun work on the less important parts of the commission. She asks if they can meet in the near future and tells Clark about a new type of cheaper of rugs Omega Workshop are now producing so that he can keep them in mind for any new purchases.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell starts by asking whether she, Clark and Duncan Grant can use their Christian names in their correspondence. She has gone to Charleston to work on Clark's commission for Duncan Grant and Vanessa Bell to decorate a large dinner service related to the theme of "Famous Women". She asks if Clark could meet with Grant in London and informs Clark that many of the items for the dinner service are already. She says she is going to work on the screen, using fish as a theme and asks Clark's opinion on this. Bell asks Clark for some family photographs and says that she is glad that he is now improved in health. In a postscript, Bell states that she is sending dinner service depictions of Marie Antoinette and the Queen of Sheba to be fired.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant thanks Clark for his recent check for a number of drawings, remarking that he "cannot believe" that they "are worth anything like that." He tells Clark that he need not return other works until it is convenient for him to do so. Grant ends by saying that Vanessa has "collected nearly all the ladies", remarking that she has even tracked down the actresses "who were difficult to track down." [These are likely to be subjects for plates from Kenneth Clark's commission for Duncan Grant and Vanessa Bell to decorate a large dinner service related to the theme of "Famous Women".]

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell writes to Clark about a screen she has been working on for her. Their mutual friend, Roger Fry, has told Bell that he doesn't think the screen she has prepared to be suitable for Clark's room. Bell asks if she can keep the one she has made and make a new one. She says she will produce for Clark a screen which is less "overpowering & less accented & perhaps even without fish!" She also suggests, on Fry's advice, to make the screen thinner. She ends by asking Clark to come and visit her and Duncan Grant.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell says she is relieved that Clark likes the screen and hopes she will get to see it in her room some time in the future. Bell apologizes that she didn't see Clark the previous week, informing Clark that she and Duncan Grant went to Sussex at the last minute. She asks when Clark and her husband, Kenneth Clark, would like to come to see the latest consignment from Wedgwood for Clark's commission from Bell and Grant to decorate a dinner service. She says that they have nearly completed the entire service save a few plates and some which need to be re-done. Bell asks Clark if she and Grant might have a tea party to show the service to some friends before giving them over to the Clarks. She ends by encouraging Clark to come for a meal at her and Grant's home.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant says that two of his artist friends, Robert Lotiron and a "M. Clairin" [probably Pierre-Eugène Clairin], are looking for works to include in an exhibition of English pictures for their "Autumn Salon" [Salon d'Automne]. He says that they would like to talk to Clark about the matter and gives him their address in Queen's Gate.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 9 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell confirms a meeting with Clark, set for the following Wednesday morning. She tells Clark that guests at a recent tea party were sorry that Clark could not attend and that he was "really wanted" at the event.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell informs Clark that she will not be in London as she planned as her son, Quentin, is ill with what is possibly whooping cough and so she is staying in Sussex to care from him. She tells Clark that if she can get to London to show Clark the Clarks' commissioned dinner service, she can telephone her. Alternatively, Bell says that if Clark telephones Clive Bell, he can tell her about Bell's plans. Bell ends by apologizes for her change of plans. In a postscript, she tells Clark that Duncan Grant is also at Charleston for a day or two.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell apologizes to Clark for not writing for so long, informing her that Bell's son has been very ill and that she is taking him to Switzerland to recover. Bell tells Clark she will make a design for her chair and that she and Duncan Grant have nearly all of the Clarks' commissioned dinner service prepared and asks whether Clark and Kenneth Clark could come to get them on Bell's return from Switzerland.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark (?)
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant says that there are still 7 plates to be completed. [These are likely to be plates from Kenneth Clark's commission for Duncan Grant and Vanessa Bell to decorate a large dinner service on the theme of "Famous Women".] He says that two plates, of Virginia Woolf and Ellen Terry, were failures and will be re-done. Grant states that three actresses are still required to "make up the dozen" and suggests making Dorothea Jordans, Anna Pavlova and Greta Garbo their subjects. Grant states that "two beauties are wanted" and proposes Emma, Lady Hamilton and "1933" before asking whether any other figures would be preferred to these.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant is responding to a letter by Clark on behalf of Vanessa Bell. He invites Clark and his wife to tea on the following Tuesday to show them their commissioned decorated dinner service. He asks if they could bring some photographs of their family as they will be "a great help."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant thanks Clark for his letter and check for £75. He has enclosed a receipt drawn up by Vanessa Bell which shows Clark's total to be £85 but says that, as the pair still have to finish a number of plates for Clark's commissioned dinner service, Clark can wait to pay the remaining £10 until they are completed. He says that he is glad that Clark likes "the set" [a dinner service?] in his own house and trusts that their were no breakages. Grant relays a message from Bell to say that she and Grant would like to visit the Clarks on the 22nd. Grant says he has to be in London early on Monday morning and asks if he could stay with Clark on Sunday evening.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell thanks Clark for her invitation to dinner and for arranging to send a car for her and Duncan Grant, adding that if it is "tiresome" for Clark to send the car, Bell and Grant can make their own way to the Clarks' home. Bell says she is "so sorry" that the Clarks have been worried about their son, Alan, and thanks Clark for her kind wishes for Bell's own son, Quentin, who has now recovered from his illness.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell says that she and Duncan Grant have priced 13 drawings Clark has chosen at £20 and that they would like to include more in the price. She asks Clark to "please say honestly if this is more than [he] can give." Bell thanks Clark for his invitation to a private viewing but tells him that she is very busy preparing everything for the opening of her exhibition at Lefevre Galleries in the upcoming week and will likely be unable to make it. She ends by saying that Clark is always welcome in the evenings at Fitzroy Street.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell apologizes for not being able to "help about Bianca Weiss" but says that the only hotel she knows is the Etoile [in Paris, possibly.] Bell's daughter, Angelica, has been ill with scarlet fever and so she has been unable to go to the opera this week and hopes to perhaps go on Friday evening. She tells Clark that she will not be able to see her on Sunday but that Clive Bell and Duncan Grant would be delighted to see her. She passes on Grants thanks to Kenneth Clark for his last letter. In a postscript, Bell gives Clark directions to Charleston.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell writes to Clark regarding an exhibition of Roger Fry's works at the Courtauld Institute [perhaps after his death.] She describes the difficulty of curating the show, given the lack of space in the exhibition room(s) and Bell and Duncan Grant's desire to be sensitive to the feelings of Fry's family. She says that Fry sister, Margery, is setting out all Fry's paintings to decide which works to exhibit and Bell asks if Clark could come and give his "disinterested" opinion on what to exhibit. She proposes a time for Clark to come and see the works and, in a postscript, gives Fry another time should the original be inconvenient.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 folded sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 24 x 17 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell thanks Clark for his check, expressing her relief that he does not think it too much. Bell asks if when she is next in London she can "get at" Clark, even if just on the telephone, so that she can get Clark's advice about Duncan Grant's communications with Cunard. She ends by saying that she hopes Clark enjoys his upcoming time away from London.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 2 sheets (3 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell apologizes for bothering Clark on his holiday but does not know what to do about the incident surrounding the HMS Queen Mary so has decided, on Clive Bell's advice, to contact Clark. She says she thought that Clark was going to "let loose" the press but that the story has not been published except for in The Express. Bell says she thinks the best place to promote the story would be in The Times and says that Clive Bell has written a piece for The Listener and The New Statesmen, but that she "feels doubtful as to [these] being a good thing." Bell says that "Mr. Medley" has intervened on Duncan Grant's behalf to call on the Cunard Line to return his panels. Bell has been to visit the HMS Queen Mary and found it "most depressing", commenting that the panels that have replaced Grant's are "the worst things of all." Bell says that Clark need not reply if he thinks that Clive Bell's pieces won't have a negative impact on the incident and describes Clive's piece as "well done & very insulting to Sir Percy Bates." She ends by wishing Clark and his wife the best for their travels. [This letter pertains to the Cunard Affair, an incident in which Cunard White Star Ltd. asked Duncan Grant and Vanessa Bell to submit panels to decorate their new flagship liner RMS Queen Mary. Cunard later rejected the panels, even after their completion, and denied Grant compensation claims for loss of reputation. The affair saw prominent figures, including Kenneth Clark, give their public support to Grant and Bell.]

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell sends Clark more legal letter regarding the Cunard Affair. She mentions that Clive Bell has published a piece on the matter in The Spectator. While she does not think representatives of Cunard will have read the piece, she believes that they will have to return to Grant his completed panels now that the incident has garnered so much public attention and Grant has dropped all other claims. Bell informs Clark that Grant has been away but that she and her daughter Angelica will be staying at Fitzroy Street over the weekend and that she hopes she will meet Clark during her time in London. scopecontent.p: Bell sends Clark her solicitor's letter and Cunard's response, asking for Clark advice on whether to pursue further legal action. She ends by sending her best wishes for the recovery of the health of Clark's son, Colin. did.unittitle: Duncan Grant postcard to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 postcard : autograph letter, signed ; 10 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant says he would like to visit Clark on the following Thursday. He comments that he takes great pleasure in meeting new people and not feeling as if he has an obligation to them afterwards. On front of postcard is a reproduction of "Musée du Louvre, Sens - Intèrieur de la Cathèdrale" by J.-B. Corot.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant tells Clark that his household has just received the "terrible news" of the death of Julian Bell, son of Vanessa Bell, while working with the Red Cross in Madrid [, during the Spanish Civil War.] He says that "Vanessa has completely collapsed physically. She is in bed & very weak & can hardly eat anything." He suggests that he and Clark put off their proposed sitting as he does not know if Virginia Woolf will be able to attend and that Grant does not want to leave Bell alone. He says that the sitting will likely have to be re-commenced when his family return to London after the summer. Grant ends by saying that he hopes Clark's voyage to Constantinople will be enjoyable.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 4 sheets (4 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant says that since their morning meeting, he has come up with some suggestions for works to be included in the British Exhibition's Modern Section which he thinks will ease some of the problems the committee for the section has been facing. He recommends that works by painters influenced by Post Impressionism, including himself, Vanessa Bell and Christopher Wood, be left out and others by "the more important painters", such as Walter Sickert, be included in their place. Grant says that he believes the exhibition to be very representative of English painting up to the Impressionist era but that that these "more important painters" are under-represented. Grant admits that if space and money were no object, then he would recommend two works by a number of artists, including Roger Fry, Vanessa Bell, John Nash and Grant himself. Grant suggests that a note be made in the preface of the exhibition catalog stating that there is not enough room in the gallery space to include works from artists after a certain period, this period being defined not by date but by school or artistic movement. Grant ends by saying that he thinks he will raise these suggestions at their next meeting and asks Clark for his comments on them prior to the meeting.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant apologizes for bothering Clark but says he can only organize this "piece of business" through her. He asks if she recalls the school of painting that Claude Rogers and John Passmore [probably the Euston Road School, London] are planning to found and that she and her husband, Kenneth Clark, had suggested they send out a prospectus, the printing of which the Clarks would pay for. Grant says that, despite "endless delays", an enclosed prospectus has been proofread and the price for printing estimated to be £9. He says that the printing should be done soon so that the prospectus is ready in time to be shown to students before the holidays and asks if she could get "Miss Arnold" to phone Vanessa Bell to tell her what she thinks.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant says it was kind of Clark to buy a picture for him "in such bad times."He remarks that Agnew's or the Lefevre Gallery would have sold a similar-sized piece for around £40. Grant says he is sorry that he will not see Clark and his wife before they leave for the United States. He ends by writing: "Save for the Dictators' antics it been [illegible] here for the last 3 days."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant thanks Clark for his letter and is glad he responded in case Grant had misunderstood Clark's reading of Leonardo. He says that he and Vanessa Bell would love to spend a night with Clark and his wife and but want to settle into their new home at present. Grant gives an account of their house-moving process, remarking that "it would be difficult to leave until [they] are more or less in order." He asks that Clark tell him the latest day it would be convenient for him to host Grant and Bell.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant thanks Clark for sending his the foreword to Clark's latest publication, remarking that he is "very grateful to [Clark] for having undertaken such a task / do not know how [Grant] dared ask [Clark] to do it." He praises the style and length of the piece and says that Colin Agnew enjoyed it too. Grants ends by saying "it doesn't matter about Portsmouth", stating that his main concern was Toulon.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell tells Clark that she was sorry to miss her and Kenneth Clark during their last visit. She will return Clark's screen through Roger Fry and says that the white around the edges needs touching up and offers to do that for her in the future. Bell describes a painting that Duncan Grant did of Clark "with a stiff neck" and says if Clark doesn't like it, she can send it back.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bells tells Clark she might receive a letter from a Mrs. Diana Beaumont asking if she and her husband could visit to see Clark and Clark's art collection. They are a recently married couple and Beaumont has told Clark that she used to be a pupil of Clark's. [This could be actress Diana Beaumont and her husband, Gabriel Toyne. They were married in 1941.]

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 18 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell acknowledges Clark's sympathy note after the death of Virginia Woolf, saying that "it is a help to know that those besides those who knew her well understand what they have lost." She encourages Clark, and the younger generation, not to lose courage and laments the fact that they were not given more of a chance to get to know Woolf. She finishes the letter by wondering whether she and Clark will meet again, stating that she "hope[s] so very much."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 19 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant tells Clark that "the ladies of Lewes" [most likely Frances Byng Stamper and Caroline Lucas] are delighted that Clark has agreed to loan them some sculptures for their show, which is to be opened by the Bishop of Chichester in January. Grant remarks: "I suppose it is alright, a Bishop opening a show of nudes." Grants says that he thinks the show will be good, and names some of the other contributors to the exhibition. He asks Clark if he knows of anyone who has portable works by Brâncuși or Matisse, commenting that he has written to "Penrose" [Richard?] to ask if he could donate any Picasso sculptures. Grant references a conversation where Clark expressed a desire to commission an artist for agricultural works and suggests that Quentin Bell could perhaps produce one, having worked on Maynard Keynes's farm. Grant recommends that the picture's subject be one of "special war subjects", suggesting "the introduction of female labour" as a possible theme.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 19 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant asks Clark to let him know when Grant can visit the National Gallery to collect sculptures to be loaned to Frances Byng Stamper and whether he should bring one or two suitcases to transport them in.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 18 x 12 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: A note in top left of letter reads: "Ripe. 65." Grant apologizes for not replying to Clark's latest letter as he has been away for a few days. He says Clark's idea appeals to him and declares that, during a recent drive through the capital, he has noticed how much London has come to be "like Ancient Rome." Grant agrees to produce a work depicting St. Paul's Cathedral [likely to be St Paul's, 1941] and says he will do several sketches and drawings of the spot Clark would like represented. Grant says that he hopes Clark will visit Lewes some day and comments that Frances Byng Stamper's gallery, to which Clark has donated works, is very good. He focuses specifically about Clark's donated Matisse and Picasso.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 19 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant thanks Clark for collecting statues to be loaned to the Lewes exhibition from his country house and outlines arrangements for their transportation from London. Grant says if the person and van he has sent to collect the pieces cannot see Clark, he will come to London himself on the following Tuesday to collect the pieces.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 19 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant informs Clark that he has safely received his statues, commenting that "the Degas is a marvelous thing." Grant asks whether Clark would like to keep the statues on his insurance or to have Frances Byng Stampers insure them for the show.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 24 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant tells Clark that he would like to see her when he is in London the following week and asks her to let him know her availability in the evenings. He says he would be very pleased if his Queen Mary panels were featured in the National Gallery Restaurant and that the smaller of these would be best for the site. Grant informs Clark that many of Bell's older works are not available and she only has more recent works. Grant says that he has many of his own older works but few frames.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 24 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant tells Clark that he has spoken to Bell about producing the panels for the National Gallery Restaurant and that she is "rather thrilled with the idea." He says that if Clark still would like them to take up the job, they can make designs for scale for her approval and begin work on the panels within a month. He asks Clark if she could find a way of taking measurements of the wall where the panels will be situated. Grant remarks that he enjoyed seeing Clark and her husband, Kenneth Clark, at a recent dinner party and asks Clark to give him the address and the spelling of the name of the hostess. Grant says that he and Bell would like to "subscribe" to the death mask of John Constable.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant postcard to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 postcard : autograph letter, signed ; 9 x 14 cm

scopecontent.p: Grant says that he would like to come to lunch with Clark and "Raymond" on Wednesday 12th August. He tells Clark he will be at the National Gallery on that date at 12:45. Front of postcard is a reproduction of Andrea Mantegna's Martirio di S. Giacomo.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 18 x 12 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant says he hopes that Clark enjoyed his holiday in Wales and enquires after Clark's son. Grant asks if Clark would open an exhibition organized by "the ladies of Miller's'" but that he knows it is unlikely Clark will be able to do so. He gives Clark the train times to Lewes from London and offer Clark a bed at Grant and Vanessa Bell's home.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 24 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant thanks Clark for agreeing to come to Lewes to discuss the Miller's exhibition and for contacting Frances Byng Stamper regarding the show. Grant asks Clark about dates for his visit and asks if he can move his anticipated lecture date in Lewes to a day later so that the chemist who will be manipulating the slides can make the presentation. Grant tells Clark that he and his wife are welcome to stay at Charleston and that he will be able to work there, uninterrupted. Grant says that people are not allowed to walk on the top of the Downs near their home "because of gun practice" but that there are many other good walks in the area, remarking that Clark and his wife should bring "good stout shoes, for it may be muddy." Grant suggest that, if Clark insists on staying at an inn, he should stay at Shelley's rather than the White Shark "where beds are said to be hard" but that "Shelley's is run by a madman so do come here."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 21 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant thanks Clark for some photographs of Grant's artworks, which he describes as "much better than any [Grant] ha[s] taken before." He ends by remarking that he hopes Clark is keeping an account of how many photographs he has taken as Grant believes that there will be more of them than is necessary for one book and says that he will pay for the remainder himself.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 18 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell writes to Clark to inform him about a commission from Berwick Church, Sussex for Bell and Duncan Grant to decorate the chapel. She says that she and Grant succeeded in convincing the clergymen to seek expert advice. Bell tells Clark that Grant has created a sketch of his preliminary ideas which she imagines will come to Clark. In a postscript, Bell tells Clark that the sketch "is meant to be for a flat painted wood."

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant asks if Clark thinks the National Gallery photographer has finished with some of his works and, if so, says that he will come to London to pick them up and take them back to Lewes.
