did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell has received measurements for an interior decoration project. [This is likely to refer to Duncan Grant and Bell's 1944 decoration of the Devonshire Hill School in Tottenham, at the request of the Council for the Encouragement of Music and the Arts and the British Institute of Adult Education.] She discusses whether she and Grant might use a pre-primed canvas and asks Clark about the expense and availability of primer for canvases. She apologizes for bothering Clark and tells her that she and Grant plan to design the decoration around the story of Cinderella.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 18 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant reminds Clark about a list of lithographers he sent him and adds that Grant has now been promised further examples by Théodore Géricault and Eugène Delacroix from the Colnaghi art dealership, as well as an example from Jean-Baptise-Camille Corot. He states that they have not been able to source an example of Renoir. Grant asks Clark if he could let him know what pieces he can lend him, especially those of Graham Sutherland, for inclusion in a catalog and gives Clark the date of the exhibition and instructions for leaving loaned items in a place where Grant can pick them up. Grant comments that he thinks the exhibition will be "rather interesting" and remarks upon the cheapness of lithographs.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 17 x 13 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant explains that an exhibition of lithographs at Miller's has been delayed as the catalog takes a week to print. He asks Clark if he could donate lithographs by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Graham Sutherland and John Piper and that a representative from Lewes will be at the National Gallery on Saturday in case they are available. Grant says that the Strachey family are trying to get permission for the Bussy family, who are in Nice, to come to England. One of the family members has given Clark's name as a sponsor and Grant asks that if "anyone asks [Clark] about him please give him a good character."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant informs Clark that Miller's will have a portrait and interiors with figures exhibition. Grant says that when he was at the National Gallery looking for his own works, he found a portrait of Clark and another of Clark and another man by Coldstream which he asks Clark if he could lend to Miller's. He says that while the show is planned to tour other places, Clark could withdraw his pieces after three weeks. Grant relays to Clark that he met "Raymond" who told him that he and Clark had some difficulty in correcting a proof in color of one of Grant's works. He asks if it might be better for artists to go through colored photographs with the photographer before they are cleared for publication. Grant has been thinking about a forthcoming lithograph exhibition by the Committee for Encouragement of Music and the Arts (CEMA) and asks whether the artists working on the exhibition be given a chance to working "directly on the stone" and praises the work of a young artist training in lithography at the Central School. Grant says that he would not like to do a lithograph himself and asks that Clark "do not press it at the C.E.M.A panel meeting." He ends by saying that Clark does not need to reply by letter but can answer his questions when they meet in person the following Friday.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 folded sheet (3 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 21 x 26 cm, folded to 21 x 13 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell says that she and Grant are sorry they did not see Clark and his wife before the Clarks left for Portugal. Bell writes to seek Clark's advice about starting a new, alternative version of Omega Workshops which produces designs for textiles, wallpapers and rugs. Bell says that they do not want to open a shop but to "set manufacturers to produce stuffs" which is sold either by the manufacturers themselves to shops or by their company to shops. She says that their main obstacle is capital as manufacturers would only be able to front a small part of the cost. Bell says that they would take a small premises in London as an office for the company. She emphasizes that she does not want financing from Clark but asks if he would like to be part of the company. Bell expresses her and Grant's desire to support younger artists through the company.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell asks if Clark really does plan to gift her painting Pheasants to the Tate and asks whether she can give another painting in exchange, as she has many things she made during her time in Rome. She hopes that Clark will come and see Duncan Grant's most recent decoration, remarking that thus far Grant has been relying "mostly upon [Bell's] criticisms" and that Clark's input would be useful. Grant has been designing textiles for a number of nurseries and wonders if he should ask whether Warner's on Moorgate Street would be interested in them and asks if Clark would write to them on their behalf. She ends by suggesting that "getting the Princess Marina to have a nursery done on patriotic grounds!". She ends by saying that she hopes to see Clark on the following Thursday.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 folded sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 21 x 27 cm, folded to 21 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant asks whether Clark would give a lecture at Miller's and assures Clark that he can discuss whatever he likes. Grant tells Clark that he can spend the night at his and Vanessa Bell's house after the lecture. Grant adds that he and Bell are going to Paris in the next week "for as long as [their] $35 last."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 19 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant has sent Clark a bookmark as a Christmas card and offers her "best wishes for 1949."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant apologizes that the weekend that he and Vanessa Bell had arranged to visit Clark and Clark clashes with a visit to Grant and Bell's home by Desmond McCarthy and "Raymond" [Mortimer?]. He ends by saying how much he enjoyed a recent party where Clark was a guest and apologizing for his penmanship.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 21 x 16 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grants says he is distressed by Clark's most recent letter saying that he "cannot risk an expedition" to "these parts" (probably the United Kingdom) as his wife is ill. Grant ends by saying that he hopes the weather is mild for the couple to come home.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Jane and Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 17 x 13 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant is delighted with a gift given to him and Vanessa by Clark [likely to be Clark's book The Nude: a study in ideal form]. Grant goes on to say that he and Clive Bell have been having heated discussions at home and that "we are all, in various degrees, interested in Sex and Art." He ends by wishing Clark a "rather early" happy Christmas.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane and Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell thanks Clark for his recent present [probably Clark's book The Nude: a study in ideal form] but says that is has divided their "apparently united household" and that it is she who has "had to give way" to Grant to read it. She says that Clark has "written something which is evidently going to stir us all up and make us talk and think and dispute and try to find out what we really feel about the things we care most for." She ends by saying that though Clark's "castle is unapproachable", she hopes that she can still meet and talk with him some time in the future.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 18 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell has been "trying to copy the Rembrandt" woman and asks Clark if she can send it to her to hang in her "great castle." She apologizes that it is not nicer but believes that once it is ready for varnish, it might look better.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 folded sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 21 x 26 cm, folded to 21 x 13 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell thanks Clark for his recent present of his book [perhaps Looking at Pictures] and says that it has generated a great deal of debate between Bell, Duncan Grant and Clive Bell. She says that while Grant is "inclined to stick up for the finished painting" while she and Clive feel that the sketch has a "greater understanding of the big relationships." Bell tells Clark that she hopes they can all meet again and talk about art.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell thanks Clark for the copy she sent him of his latest book [Kenneth Clark's 1960 book Looking at Pictures.] Bell says she is glad that Clark dedicated the book to Roger Fry. Bell says that she and Duncan Grant will be staying at friends' home in London and asks if Clark might visit them there.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 18 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant thanks Clark for his note of sympathy on the event of Vanessa Bell's death, saying that he finds letters "from people expressing their affection and admiration for Vanessa although they of course in a way add to one's sense of general loss, give one some courage to face up to one's own desolation." He says that Bell died peacefully and "without pain" and expresses sympathy for Clive Bell who has only just been able to come to the house. Grant ends by saying that he is sorry that Clark has been ill and states that Clark "must get strong again to resist such things."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 18 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant thanks Clark for his note of sympathy on the event of Vanessa Bell's death, telling her that her memories of Bell give him great pleasure. He comments that "several people in their letters have remembered [Bell's] sense of humour. [Grant] now realise[s] of course that this is true but [he] always took it for granted." Grant says that Bell had been declining physically in the last year but that he is sure that she was happy and had been working on a painting exhibition towards the end of her life. Grant tells Clark that he is sorry that Kenneth Clark has been ill and that he hopes they enjoy their time in Arano [, Spain] and that one of his friends adored the village when they visited. He ends by writing "I am very much interested to hear of Colm's romantic wedding."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 26 x 21 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant has just arrived home after spending some time in France. He says that he met Joe Ackerley [J. R. Ackerley] in the street and passed on Clark's message for Grant that he had bought a portrait by Vanessa Bell, news which Grant is delighted by. Grant is happy that Clark thought a recent exhibition was well done, noting that Clive Bell thought it "overcrowded" but that Edward le Bas though it "well arranged." He tells Clark it is kind of Clark and his wife to want to meet with him and asks if he can come to Saltwood for a night.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 26 x 21 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant says he has been in London and so has only just received Clark's last letter. He tells her he would be delighted to visit Saltwood on July 27th. Grant says that Quentin Bell and his family will be staying at Charleston on their way to France. In a postscript, Grant justifies his writing to Saltwood as opposed to London as she "will more likely to be there."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 18 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant thanks Clark for her invitation to visit and says he will stay on the last Saturday of August. He signs off by saying that he hopes she will enjoy her time in Edinburgh.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 18 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant is "horrified" by Clark's recent suffering during an illness but that she "seemed wonderfully recovered." He says that she really should have encouraged Grant not to visit her at Saltwood but admits that "selfishly" he is glad that she did not. He describes his time at Saltwood, praising its beauty, remarking on how "charming" their daughter, Colette is and commenting on Kenneth Clark's kindness despite "all his troubles." Grant says he was very impressed by Clark's recent Rembrandt studies and asks Clark to encourage Clark to publish his findings. Grant describes his journey home as "stormy but successful" and send his best wishes to Clark for her full recovery.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 18 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant thanks Clark for his "noble present" [probably Clark's book Ruskin Today] which Grant is presently "deep in reading it with enormous pleasure." He notes that, until recently, Grant and his generation have not taken well to the writing of John Ruskin but questions why he was so "unsympathetic to Michael Angelo, Constable, Whistler etc." Grant also says that Ruskin's The Elements of Drawing outraged him as a youngster because it said that one should always shade heads from left to right. He remarks that he finds Ruskin's social writings "very sympathetic." In a postscript, Grant send his love to Elizabeth Jane Clark.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 18 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant tells Clark he has been thinking a great deal since their "confidential talk" they had about "the difficulties of becoming a lord." He says that he thinks he and Clark in agreement that if there was any possibility of Clark not being able to say what he thinks, he should decline the honor. However, Grant declares that having read Bertrand Russell's most recent book it would appear that receiving an establishment honour does not mean that one always has to give way to the establishment.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell thanks Clark for the return of the screen she had made for her and says that the fish are now painted out so she hopes the "later attempt will be more suitable." Bell says that she and Grant are going to Charleston on June 8th and invites Clark and Kenneth Clark to spend the night with them there on June 9th. She comments that they can easily visit Bognor Regis from there and that Bell and Duncan Grant could easily meet them from the town of Glynde. Bell tells Clark that they do not have a telephone at Charleston but that Clark can send her a telegram using the address "Charleston Firle." She adds, "if [the Clarks] come one of [Grant or Bell] will be in waiting at Glynde after the opera, so look out for the most disreputable of[...]cars." Bell assures Clark that if they arrive earlier in the day, she and Grant can meet them in Lewes. Bell says that she envies the Clarks' time in Venice and tells Clark that Grant's latest show has just finished, at which he sold thirty pieces.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell tells Clark how much she and Duncan Grant enjoyed their day with her and her husband, Kenneth Clark. She describes the Clarks' castle as being like one in a "fairytale" and commends their upkeep of their home. She comments that she and Grant got lost in the rain on their way to visit the Clarks.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell says she and Duncan Grant were sorry not to see Clark and Clark before they left for their travels but that it was probably just as well as Bell has a cold and both she and Grant have been kept busy with work. Bell wishes Clark good bye and says she hopes they enjoy their travels.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The top of this letter has a note [perhaps written by Clark] saying "keep for me." Bell gives Clark the name and address of the dentist who treats her children. She goes on to describe the dentist's "peculiarities" including his "virulent Christian" beliefs, his dislike of Americans and his assumption that Bell is a paragon of "domestic virtue." Bell says that he has been treating her for twenty five years and that she has "never had a moment's toothache or had a tooth out." In a postscript, Bell remarks that the dentist is quite expensive but that if patients think his prices too much he charged three quarters of his fees.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell comments on the "magnificence" of Clark's Christmas present to her and Duncan Grant. She says that she and Grant are not able to come in to London until next week as they are at Charleston but that she hopes they will see Clark and his wife in the next week.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell says she is glad that Clark enjoyed her recent exhibition and says that, as she hasn't had much time to spend with the finished exhibition, she hopes Clark will tell her about her work and "how [she might] go on." Bell is bringing Clark some pictures she hopes he likes. She says that Clark's wife, in a previous letter, wrote that she had enclosed a check for Bell but that the check had not been included.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 18 x 14 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell thanks Clark for helping Clive Bell to attend an appointment at a clinic where he had to undergo an emergency operation. She tells Clark that Duncan Grant has been to Clive but that she is unable to go herself as she "can hardly walk!" She hopes that people in London will bring Clive books and says she will write to Clark again if there is any news on Clive's condition.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell has been asked by Clark's wife to send him a bill before they go away. Bell explains that the couple haven't received their portrait because she has to speak with "Macdonald" about pricing of work so that her charges are not vastly different from his but that "in consequence they may be more than [Clark] think[s] reasonable." Bell says that if Clark does think the price unreasonable, he should tell her as she is willing to work for Clark for less. She tells him that the prices she suggests for the works are "£50 for the portrait and £40 for the flowers" and that she will look at getting a frame for the portrait when Clark is absent.

did.unittitle: Vanessa Bell letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bell is glad that Clark enjoyed her recent show, which she says was quite difficult to put together and resulted in her running into some trouble with other artists. Bell tells Clark she is sorry that his wife, Elizabeth Jane Clark, has been ill and invites the couple to make use of Charleston, if it would be helpful. Bell wishes that Clark would add color to the walls of the new sculpture galleries at the Tate and says that she and Duncan Grant are primed to be "let loose with coloured paper patterns."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Jane Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 14 x 9 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant says that he agrees with Clark about wanting to live closer to neighbors. He says that he is sorry that Clark has been unwell. Grant ends by saying that he has just finished penning a letter to Clark's husband, Kenneth Clark, which is "ill spelled and ill expressed."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant apologizes for being "remiss", explaining that he only just returned to England to find that he had missed a number of Clark's publications. He asks if they will be printed separately and hopes they will be at least in the Radio Times. Grant asks after Clark's wife, Elizabeth Jane Clark, and says he has not recovered since his time in Africa. He ends by apologizes for his bad writing and giving his love to Clark.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant writes to Clark to tell him how impressed the "ladies of Miller's" are by Clark's donated works for their show and that they were directly sent to them via a National Gallery attendant. He hopes that Clark was not put to too much trouble of having a case made. Grant says that he is glad that Clark's wife, Elizabeth Jane Clark, can make use of pictures by himself and Vanessa Bell, giving them the chance to give people pleasure. He informs Clark that they did not send Bell's large plasterboard work for fear it would be damaged in transportation but that they are happy to bring it to Clark if she thinks it useful. He ends by saying that a "Mr Baker", a carpenter from Lewes, enjoyed Clark's lecture at Miller's "enormously and that everyone round him at the end were crying out for more."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant asks if Clark would lend the portraits Grant produced of Clark and his wife to an exhibition at the Lefevre Gallery. He says he will telephone Clark the following morning for an answer and asks if Clark could leave an answer if he will be out. On the verso, another person has written a note to send a cable to "Garnett Evergreen Baltimore (Maryland)". The note says that the writer was delighted to "see you both". It ends by saying "Unable find you summer house owingto uncertain worldd of conditions. Send cheque away."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant thanks Clark for the cheque for £30, remarking that it is "more than it should be but [Grant is] more incapable than you of doing the sum - so [Grant] benefit[s]." Grant is back in Charleston after a spell in London and says he is sorry that he and Vanessa Bell cannot see Clark and says that they should try to meet again before Clark's wife goes to the United States.

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant has enclosed a note from "Wilton about the carpet" and says he is not sure how Clark will respond, commenting that if Clark does not mind waiting as Wilton suggests then someone might appear who would like it. He ends by saying that he feels "very sorry about the whole business."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant recommends that Clark go to "see the children at work at the [illegible - could be "Country"] Hall", remarking that "they & the things they do are enchanting." He says that he has written a letter to "Morris" about decorating the nursery with the Queen Mary. In a postscript, Grant suggest that it [the work at the Hall?] might interest Clark's wife and soon and relays a message from Vanessa Bell asking if Clark wanted "those drawings."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (1 page) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant thanks Clark for his letter and check for £100, remarking that he is glad that Clark thinks it a fair price. He says he hopes he will see Clark and his wife soon and asks if he can telephone Clark's wife, Elizabeth Jane Clark, about whether or not he can visit her one evening. Grant ends by apologizes for his "awful pen."

did.unittitle: Duncan Grant letter to Kenneth Clark
did.physdesc: 1 sheet (2 pages) : autograph letter, signed ; 23 x 18 cm

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Grant opens by apologizing for "bothering" Clark about money. Grant acknowledges that he and Clark had agreed that Clark would pay him for his portrait of Clark's wife, Elizabeth Jane Clark, and his self-portrait upon the former's completion but asks if Clark might pay him for the self portrait now because Grant's "Bank Manager tells [him he] cannot be overdrawn any more." He also comments that Clark had said that he would pay Grant £10 for a failed carpet design. Grant suggests the price of his self portrait to be £50, remarking that he thinks dealers would ask for such a price for a similar piece, although asks Clark to be frank if he thinks the price too high. Grant says that Vanessa Bell is still physically weak but getting stronger and is improving with her time in the countryside with her children. He ends by asking Clark to give Grant's love to Clark's wife and says that he hopes they enjoy their imminent travels.
